context: letters from J. D. Hooker, which you are answering
exchanges:
When I read your letter & came to the part that said you could work an hour a day, my heart leaped— I am so glad, & like the boys I say ‘Oh my how jolly—’

No one believes Karsten— he has been asked to come forward & would not: I heard the subject discussed by Decaisne & Naudin when in Paris, & by Braun & others at Vienna in 1858 I think   Karsten is a very bad observer— Braun you know I think it was who found a pollen tube in the ovary, but attributed it to some other plant.— I have often selected a plant of Cœleb. to operate upon, but one & another thing always put it off! I think Brauns paper is in Ann. Sc. Nat. but am not sure.

Your observation on the undoubted offspring of species simulating hybrids is a surprizing fact, & I cannot understand it— have you ever had 2 or more such pseudo-hybrids from one capsule or plant; or produced the same pseudo-hybrid twice.

John Scotts observations were always too much for me— but I do not like to be churlish in my estimate of success in a line of enquiry I have not followed—& could only be guided to a judgment by appearances. Then too I was suspicious of results obtained by snatches at a time when he should have been doing something else & was always in dread of being caught.

I would let Palestine alone just now— we have shipped an explorer off, & if at all successful more funds will be wanted & then will be the time.

Anderson has given Scott a capital appt. at Calcutta   I hope he has squared with you.

I am diverted at your quandary about membership of societies—as it was only yesterday that I got a hint that I had not had the civility to acknowledge one that I had forgotten all about— Latterly I have taken to send my titles as they come to Kippist who inserts them in the Linnæan list— I do not like to parade them in the Royal, & it is not polite to the said Academies to ignore them altogether   The Linnæan list seemed to me a modest way of embalming them & if I had only kept it up, it would have been a means of reference useful to myself. The Berlin, St. Petersburgh & Austrian Academys’ are real honors, also the Bavarian.— The French Institute is no longer worth having quoad Correspondence but membership is the greatest continental honor that can be passed on a foreigner.

I am surprized at your election to Edinbh. R. S.—the Edinburgh people being as prejudiced partial & unfair as the Parisian.

The Berlin Academy does not send proceedings to Foreign correspondents or members I believe.

By all means sign Haasts paper when drawn up, I shall—but I am in a bit of a fix here   Haast asked me to draw up & sign his paper, being no Geologist I transferred it to Murchison, who being then on Council transferred it to Ramsay, who will do it.— I however felt very strongly that if Haast is F.R.S. before Hector it will be a bad thing. Because 1. Hectors claims are far higher as previously Geologist to American Expedition; 2. Hector is Director Genl. of Geolog. Survey of all N. Z. & high above Haast who is only provincial Geologist to Canterbury. 3. There is an ugly attack made on Haast in the Colony, for appropriating some other mans facts & theories bodily. Considering all these facts, & as a friend to both parties, & knowing that modesty alone kept Hector from putting his name forward—I wrote consulted confidentially Ramsay & Lyell, & both agreeing, I wrote to Hector the other day saying that I would have him proposed, though there will not be time to get his answer or approval.— I was also influenced by the fear that Haast was not elected (& I hear he would not be) the first year & Hector comes forward the next with Haasts name still up, the collision would be awkward   Hector I think would get in at once— Haast I think not, there being a more deserving Geologist on the list; but one not superior to Hector.

I am really extremely well though still a little stiff in the joints— I have taken to Gardening i.e. laying out walks lawns shrubberies & planting trees &c, with enthusiasm

I shall look to go down to Bromley at an early Sunday— Frances cannot till the bairns go back to school.

Ever Yrs affec | J D Hooker

I send a quip to amuse the boys.

I do not think I quite understand the Hybrid affair.

I had a talk with Oliver about Cœlebogyne. He says that Baillon found a stamen here & there on the female flowers; & O. seems to disbelieve the “Virgin Mary plant”, as its discoverer Allan Cunningham called it. I examined many flowers without finding them, as did R. Brown, Decaisne, J. Smith, A. Braun & others.

The difficulty of enclosing the flowers in gauze is that they grow quite down in the nests of the rigid leaves, & that not 1 in 100 ever ripens a seed. This, & the fact that every ovary is 3 celled & only 1 cell usually produces a ripe seed, renders the search for pollen tubes interminable. I tried a great many in vain.

Ever aff yrs | J D Hooker

I take for granted you know that Lyell is most good naturedly working to get me the Copley medal, & after his funny & not-at-all-agreeable-to-me fashion, telling me all about it, & getting me to send him copies of my papers to send to Sir H. Holland, who he wants to saddle with me. Of course I must not tell him so, but it is God’s-truth, that not only shall I never think I deserve it if I get it; but that if I did deserve it, it would be far too dear at the cost of an after dinner Speech. These are things however which must take their courses

I write a line to say, firstly, to say how rejoiced I am that there is a good chance of seeing you here for a Sunday: do keep to so good an intention— it will be a real joy to me.— Secondly to thank for for information about Karsten & the case of parthenogenesis, about which I became very curious. It is jolly to hear of you working in the garden & very good for mind & body.

I will explain about my so-called hybrids of Lythrum when we meet.—

I had heard & talked with Sir H. H. & Lyell about the C. medal (which I knew you would not care very much about, tho’ that is no reason for your friends not wishing it most earnestly) & it was very foolish in Lyell, who, I believe originated the idea this year, speaking to you about it. If I had my way it shd. not be mooted in Council this year with so very few naturalists of any kind (deserving the name) on the Council.—

Yours affectionately | C. Darwin

As for your thinking that you do not deserve the C. Medal, that I declare is mere insanity.—
